tools.description: Execute a bash command (`bash -c`) and return its stdout/stderr. Each call runs in a fresh shell: no state (cwd, variables, functions) persists between calls — pass `workdir` instead of using `cd`. Non-zero exits are reported as `[exit code: N]`. Current harness environment facts are exposed through managed `$DSH_*` variables; inspect them when needed. Commands may run under a file sandbox; a blocked file operation is reported as `[sandbox: file access denied under <mode> mode]` — a policy denial, not a bug in the command; do not retry another way. Long output is truncated to its tail; the full output is saved to a file whose path is reported when available. Set `run_in_background: true` for long-running commands: the call returns a job id immediately; read its output with `job_output` and stop it with `job_kill`. Attempting a command the sandbox may deny is safe and expected: run it and read the marker rather than assuming the denial. When a command is denied and a wider mode would let it succeed, escalate immediately in the same turn — the one sanctioned exception to a denial: retry the exact same command once with `sandbox_permissions` (the narrowest wider mode that suffices) plus a one-sentence `justification`. Do not detour through chat to ask permission first — the approval prompt raised by that retry is how the user consents. If the session states approval prompts are disabled, there is no exception: a denial is final — do not set `sandbox_permissions`. Never escalate speculatively: ground the request in a real denial — normally the one this command just hit; escalating up front is fine only when this session already denied the same access. A rejected escalation is final for that command — stop and explain, never work around it — but it does not forbid attempting or escalating other commands later.

A line is then read as one of these, in this order. 19: 20: A line of three or more backticks with no further backtick on it opens a fenced code block, and its info string is the rest of the line, trimmed, of which the first word is used. The fence closes at the first later line that is nothing but backticks, at least as many as the opening had, and everything between the two is content. A fence that never closes fails. A blank line ends whatever block was open. `#` to `######` followed by a space is a heading of that level, over the trimmed rest of the line. `- ` at the very start of a line is a bullet item, unless a paragraph is already open, in which case it is one of that paragraph's lines. 23: 
24: ## Inline
25: 
26: A backslash before one of `` \ ` * [ ] ( ) `` writes that character literally. A backtick pair is a code span, with its content escaped. `**` pairs make `` and `*` pairs make ``, each rendering its content inline. `[text](url)` is a link, with the text rendered inline and the url escaped for the attribute. An unmatched marker is literal text. Everything else is escaped for HTML.
27: 
28: ## Modes
29: 
30: - `html` writes the rendered document.
31: - `outline` writes one line per heading, ` `.
32: 
33: ## Failures
34: 
35: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. An unterminated fence is `error: line N: unterminated code fence`, naming the line the fence opened on. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
36: 
37: ## Known gaps
38: 
39: A list is flat: an indented `- ` is a paragraph line, not a nested item. There are no reference links, so `[text][label]` is literal text and a `[label]: url` line renders as a paragraph. Fence content is copied out verbatim, so a `<` in a code block escapes into the surrounding HTML and a document that shows HTML in a code block renders wrong.

`jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. ---README---
# jobq

A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.

## Layout

| File | What it owns |
| --- | --- |
| `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
| `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
| `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
| `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |

`test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.

## The log

One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.

```
limit 2 10
job build 5 ok
job flaky 3 fail ok
submit 0 build
submit 0 flaky
```

`limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.

## The simulation

The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.

## Modes

- `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
- `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.

A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.

## Failures

Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.

## Known gaps

A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

10: /** Report one failure the way the specification words it, and stop. */
11: function fail(message) {

14: }

16: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
17: const mode = argv[0]
18: if (!['trace', 'summary'].includes(mode) || argv.length !== 1) fail(USAGE)
19: 
20: const policy = {}
21: let parsed

23:   parsed = parse(splitLines(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')), policy)

25:   if (!(error instanceof LogError)) throw error
26:   fail(error.line === 0 ? error.message : `line ${error.line}: ${error.message}`)
27: }
28: 
29: const { attempts, end } = run(parsed.jobs, parsed.submissions, policy)
30: const out = []
31: if (mode === 'trace') {
32:   for (const one of attempts) out.push(`${one.start} ${one.id} attempt=${one.attempt} ${one.outcome} finish=${one.finish}`)
33: } else {
34:   for (const { id } of [...parsed.submissions].sort((left, right) => (left.id < right.id ? -1 : 1))) {
35:     const own = attempts.filter(one => one.id === id)

1: /** The log grammar: the directives, and the failures each one words. */
2: 
3: const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /**
44:  * Parse the job log.
45:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
46:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the policy the log sets, edited in place.
47:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
48:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
49:  */
50: export function parse(lines, policy) {
51:   const jobs = new Map()
52:   const submissions = []
53:   const submitted = new Map()
54:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
55:     const line = index + 1
56:     const text = raw.trim()
57:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
58:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
59:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
60:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected limit <starts> <window>')
61:       if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
62:       policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }
63:     } else if (words[0] === 'job') {
64:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
65:       const id = words[1]
66:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
67:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
68:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
69:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
70:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)
71:       }
72:       jobs.set(id, { id, duration, outcomes: words.slice(3) })
73:     } else if (words[0] === 'submit') {
74:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected submit <at> <id>')
75:       const at = count(line, 'at', words[1])
76:       const id = words[2]
77:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
78:       if (submitted.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is submitted twice`)
79:       submitted.set(id, line)
80:       submissions.push({ id, at })
81:     } else {
82:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
83:     }
84:   }
85:   for (const { id } of submissions) {
86:     if (!jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(0, `unknown job ${id}`)
87:   }
88:   return { jobs, submissions }
89: }

1: /** The simulation: one worker and a rate limit on starts. */
2: 
3: import { createClock } from './clock.js'
4: 
5: /**
6:  * Run every submission to a verdict.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
8:  * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
9:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the rate limit in force.
10:  * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started and the clock at the end.
11:  */
12: export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
13:   const clock = createClock()
14:   const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
15:   const attempts = []
16:   const starts = []
17:   while (queued.length > 0) {
18:     let pick = 0
19:     for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
20:       const best = queued[pick]
21:       if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
22:     }
23:     const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
24:     clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
25:     if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
26:       const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
27:       if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
28:     }
29:     const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
30:     const start = clock.now()
31:     starts.push(start)
32:     const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
33:     const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
34:     const finish = start + job.duration
35:     clock.advanceTo(finish)
36:     attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
37:   }
38:   return { attempts, end: clock.now() }
39: }

1: /** The log grammar: the directives, and the failures each one words. */
2: 
3: const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /** Parse a `limit` directive's words into the policy, or throw the failure it names. */
44: function parseLimit(line, words, policy) {
45:   if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected limit <starts> <window>')
46:   if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
47:   policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }
48: }
49: 
50: /** Parse a `retry` directive's words into the policy, or throw the failure it names. */
51: function parseRetry(line, words, policy) {
52:   if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected retry <max> <base>')
53:   if (policy.retry !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'retry is declared twice')
54:   const max = positive(line, 'max', words[1])
55:   const base = count(line, 'base', words[2])
56:   policy.retry = { max, base }
57: }
58: 
59: /**
60:  * Parse a policy file: `limit` and `retry` lines only, under the log's own grammar.
61:  * @param {string[]} lines - the policy file's own lines.
62:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}, retry?: {max: number, base: number}}} policy - the policy, edited in place.
63:  * @returns {void}
64:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
65:  */
66: export function parsePolicy(lines, policy) {
67:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
68:     const line = index + 1
69:     const text = raw.trim()
70:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
71:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
72:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
73:       parseLimit(line, words, policy)
74:     } else if (words[0] === 'retry') {
75:       parseRetry(line, words, policy)
76:     } else {
77:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
78:     }
79:   }
80: }
81: 
82: /**
83:  * Parse the job log.
84:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
85:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}, retry?: {max: number, base: number}}} policy - the policy the log sets, edited in place.
86:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
87:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
88:  */
89: export function parse(lines, policy) {
90:   const jobs = new Map()
91:   const submissions = []
92:   const submitted = new Map()
93:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
94:     const line = index + 1
95:     const text = raw.trim()
96:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
97:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
98:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
99:       parseLimit(line, words, policy)
100:     } else if (words[0] === 'retry') {
101:       parseRetry(line, words, policy)
102:     } else if (words[0] === 'job') {
103:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
104:       const id = words[1]
105:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
106:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
107:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
108:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
109:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)
110:       }
111:       jobs.set(id, { id, duration, outcomes: words.slice(3) })
112:     } else if (words[0] === 'submit') {
113:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected submit <at> <id>')
114:       const at = count(line, 'at', words[1])
115:       const id = words[2]
116:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
117:       if (submitted.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is submitted twice`)
118:       submitted.set(id, line)
119:       submissions.push({ id, at })
120:     } else {
121:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
122:     }
123:   }
124:   for (const { id } of submissions) {
125:     if (!jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(0, `unknown job ${id}`)
126:   }
127:   return { jobs, submissions }
128: }

goal.objective:
`jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. 1: # jobq
2: 
3: A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
11: | `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
12: | `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |
13: 
14: `test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The log
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.
19: 
20: ```
21: limit 2 10
22: job build 5 ok
23: job flaky 3 fail ok
24: submit 0 build
25: submit 0 flaky
26: ```
27: 
28: `limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.
29: 
30: ## The simulation
31: 
32: The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.
33: 
34: ## Modes
35: 
36: - `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
37: - `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.
38: 
39: A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.
40: 
41: ## Failures
42: 
43: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
44: 
45: ## Known gaps
46: 
47: A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

(End of file - total 47 lines)
</content>

1: /** The log grammar: the directives, and the failures each one words. */
2: 
3: const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /**
44:  * Parse the job log.
45:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
46:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the policy the log sets, edited in place.
47:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
48:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
49:  */
50: export function parse(lines, policy) {
51:   const jobs = new Map()
52:   const submissions = []
53:   const submitted = new Map()
54:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
55:     const line = index + 1
56:     const text = raw.trim()
57:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
58:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
59:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
60:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected limit <starts> <window>')
61:       if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
62:       policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }
63:     } else if (words[0] === 'job') {
64:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
65:       const id = words[1]
66:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
67:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
68:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
69:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
70:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)
71:       }
72:       jobs.set(id, { id, duration, outcomes: words.slice(3) })
73:     } else if (words[0] === 'submit') {
74:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected submit <at> <id>')
75:       const at = count(line, 'at', words[1])
76:       const id = words[2]
77:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
78:       if (submitted.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is submitted twice`)
79:       submitted.set(id, line)
80:       submissions.push({ id, at })
81:     } else {
82:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
83:     }
84:   }
85:   for (const { id } of submissions) {
86:     if (!jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(0, `unknown job ${id}`)
87:   }
88:   return { jobs, submissions }
89: }

1: /** The simulation: one worker and a rate limit on starts. */
2: 
3: import { createClock } from './clock.js'
4: 
5: /**
6:  * Run every submission to a verdict.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
8:  * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
9:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the rate limit in force.
10:  * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started and the clock at the end.
11:  */
12: export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
13:   const clock = createClock()
14:   const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
15:   const attempts = []
16:   const starts = []
17:   while (queued.length > 0) {
18:     let pick = 0
19:     for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
20:       const best = queued[pick]
21:       if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
22:     }
23:     const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
24:     clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
25:     if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
26:       const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
27:       if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
28:     }
29:     const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
30:     const start = clock.now()
31:     starts.push(start)
32:     const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
33:     const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
34:     const finish = start + job.duration
35:     clock.advanceTo(finish)
36:     attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
37:   }
38:   return { attempts, end: clock.now() }
39: }

goal.objective:
`jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. Do not modify anything under test/ or package.json, and add no dependencies: node_modules must not exist. The standard is `node --test test/*.test.js` passing in the workspace root. This task is also judged on inputs you do not see: a validator runs your program on its own held-back cases and compares the exit code and output byte for byte. The visible tests cover the main paths only. Implement the written specification, including every corner it states, rather than the behaviour the visible tests happen to pin down.

`conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>`; `dump` takes one path, `get` a path and a key, and `load` and `origin` exactly two paths. 1: # conflayers
2: 
3: A configuration loader with no dependencies. It reads INI files, knows a fixed schema of settings, and answers what one of them is set to.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/ini.js` | the INI grammar and the refusals it words, as `IniError`, each with a line and a column |
11: | `src/schema.js` | `SETTINGS`, the known settings with their declared type and default text |
12: | `src/layer.js` | `merge`, which stacks layers so that the last one to set a key wins |
13: 
14: `test/conflayers.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the INI files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The INI grammar
17: 
18: A line is trimmed first. An empty one, and one beginning with `#` or `;`, is ignored. `[name]` opens a section, and a section may be opened more than once. Anything else is `key = value`: the text before the first `=` is the key, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A key outside a section keeps its own name; a key inside one is prefixed with the section name and a dot, so `port` under `[server]` is `server.port`. A name and a key are one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. Nothing inside a value is special: `#` and `;` open a comment only at the start of a line.
19: 
20: ```ini
21: log.file = /var/log/app.log
22: 
23: [server]
24: port = 9090
25: ```
26: 
27: ## The schema
28: 
29: | Key | Type | Default |
30: | --- | --- | --- |
31: | `log.file` | string | (empty) |
32: | `log.level` | enum `debug`, `info`, `warn`, `error` | `info` |
33: | `log.rotate` | boolean | `true` |
34: | `retry.attempts` | integer | `3` |
35: | `retry.backoff` | duration | `250ms` |
36: | `server.host` | string | `localhost` |
37: | `server.port` | integer | `8080` |
38: | `server.timeout` | duration | `30s` |
39: | `server.tls` | boolean | `false` |
40: | `tags` | list | (empty) |
41: 
42: The types are declared but nothing here enforces them yet: every mode below prints the raw text as the file wrote it.
43: 
44: ## Modes
45: 
46: - `dump <file>` prints `<key>=<raw text>` for every schema key in ascending order, falling back to the schema default for a key the file leaves out. A key the schema does not know is ignored.
47: - `get <file> <key>` prints the raw text of one setting, or its default. A key outside the schema is refused.
48: 
49: ## Failures
50: 
51: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure carries the position it was read at, as `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: <message>`, where the column counts characters of the raw line from 1, leading whitespace included. The messages are `expected "]"`, reported one past the line's last non-space character; `expected a section name` and `invalid section name <name>`, at the name's first character; `expected a section header or key = value` and `invalid key <key>`, at the line's first non-space character; `expected a key`, at the `=`; and `key <key> is set twice`, at the line's first non-space character. A file that cannot be read is refused as `error: cannot read <path>`, an unknown key as `error: unknown setting <key>`, and a malformed argument list with the usage line.
52: 
53: ## Known gaps
54: 
55: Only one file is ever read, so the `merge` primitive stacks a single layer and nothing overrides anything. Nothing reads the environment. The declared types do nothing: `server.port = eighty` loads as happily as `server.port = 80`, and a caller has to coerce the text itself. `IniError` carries a position, but the parse result does not, so nothing downstream could say where a bad value was written.

</content>

1: /** The INI reader: dotted keys and the raw text of each value. */
2: 
3: const NAME = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: 
5: /** One refusal of an INI line, carrying the 1-based line and column it was read at. */
6: export class IniError extends Error {
7:   /**
8:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line.
9:    * @param {number} column - the 1-based column of the raw line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, column, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'IniError'
15:     this.line = line
16:     this.column = column
17:   }
18: }
19: 
20: /** The 1-based column of the first non-space character of `raw`. */
21: function indent(raw) {
22:   return raw.length - raw.trimStart().length + 1
23: }
24: 
25: /**
26:  * Parse INI text into its settings.
27:  * @param {string} text - the file's whole text.
28:  * @returns {Map<string, string>} each dotted key's raw value, in the order the file writes them.
29:  * @throws {IniError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
30:  */
31: export function parse(text) {
32:   const lines = text.split('\n')
33:   if (lines.length > 0 && lines[lines.length - 1] === '') lines.pop()
34:   const values = new Map()
35:   let section = ''
36:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
37:     const line = index + 1
38:     const trimmed = raw.trim()
39:     if (trimmed === '' || trimmed.startsWith('#') || trimmed.startsWith(';')) continue
40:     if (trimmed.startsWith('[')) {
41:       if (!trimmed.endsWith(']')) throw new IniError(line, raw.trimEnd().length + 1, 'expected "]"')
42:       const name = trimmed.slice(1, -1)
43:       if (name === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, 'expected a section name')
44:       if (!NAME.test(name)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + 1, `invalid section name ${name}`)
45:       section = name
46:       continue
47:     }
48:     const split = trimmed.indexOf('=')
49:     if (split === -1) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), 'expected a section header or key = value')
50:     const key = trimmed.slice(0, split).trim()
51:     if (key === '') throw new IniError(line, indent(raw) + split, 'expected a key')
52:     if (!NAME.test(key)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `invalid key ${key}`)
53:     const full = section === '' ? key : `${section}.${key}`
54:     if (values.has(full)) throw new IniError(line, indent(raw), `key ${full} is set twice`)
55:     values.set(full, trimmed.slice(split + 1).trim())
56:   }
57:   return values
58: }

goal.objective:
`conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>`; `dump` takes one path, `get` a path and a key, and `load` and `origin` exactly two paths. `jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. In `summary`, a dead-lettered job reads `dead` in place of its last attempt's outcome; every other job reads that outcome as before.

Every mode takes an optional second argument naming a policy file, so the usage line becomes `error: usage: cli.js trace|summary|dead [<policy>]`. A policy file holds `limit` and `retry` lines and nothing else, read under the log's own grammar, with a line trimmed and an empty one or one starting with `#` ignored. It is read before the log, so its failures come first, and a directive it sets is already in force when the log is parsed: a log that sets the same directive fails at the log's own line with `limit is declared twice` or `retry is declared twice`. A policy file's own failures are worded `error: <policy>: line N: ` followed by the message the same directive would give in the log, with `unknown directive <word>` for anything that is not `limit` or `retry`, and N counting the policy file's own lines from 1. A policy file that cannot be read fails with `error: cannot read policy <path>`. Change only files under src/. 1: # jobq
2: 
3: A job-queue simulator with no dependencies. It reads a log from standard input and replays it on one worker against a clock that only moves when the simulation asks it to, so a run is the same on every machine and in every order.
4: 
5: ## Layout
6: 
7: | File | What it owns |
8: | --- | --- |
9: | `src/cli.js` | the argument forms, the mode dispatch, and how a failure is reported |
10: | `src/parse.js` | the log grammar and the refusals it words, as `LogError` |
11: | `src/queue.js` | the simulation: what starts when, and what the rate limit holds back |
12: | `src/clock.js` | `createClock`, the monotonic clock the simulation advances by hand |
13: 
14: `test/jobq.test.js` is the suite for what is already here, and `data/` holds the policy files the examples name.
15: 
16: ## The log
17: 
18: One directive per line. A line is trimmed first; an empty one and one that starts with `#` are ignored; the rest is split on runs of whitespace. Every number is an unsigned decimal integer written without a sign or a separator.
19: 
20: ```
21: limit 2 10
22: job build 5 ok
23: job flaky 3 fail ok
24: submit 0 build
25: submit 0 flaky
26: ```
27: 
28: `limit <starts> <window>` allows at most `<starts>` starts inside any window of `<window>` milliseconds, and may appear at most once. `job <id> <duration> <outcome>...` declares a job that occupies the worker for `<duration>` milliseconds and whose attempts turn out as the listed `ok` and `fail` words, the last of which repeats. An id is one or more of the characters `A` to `Z`, `a` to `z`, `0` to `9`, `_`, `.` and `-`. `submit <at> <id>` puts a declared job in the queue at that instant; a job may be submitted at most once.
29: 
30: ## The simulation
31: 
32: The clock starts at 0 and one worker runs everything. Take the queued attempt with the smallest ready time, breaking ties by submission order, and advance the clock to that ready time. If a rate limit is in force and the last `<starts>` starts all fall inside the window ending now, advance the clock to the instant the oldest of them leaves it. The attempt starts at the clock's instant and finishes `<duration>` later, and the clock advances to that finish. A job of duration 0 finishes in the instant it starts. A failed attempt is simply over: nothing here retries it.
33: 
34: ## Modes
35: 
36: - `trace` prints one line per attempt in the order the attempts started, `<start> <id> attempt=<n> <outcome> finish=<finish>`, and then a final `end <clock>` line.
37: - `summary` prints one line per submitted job in ascending id order, `<id> attempts=<n> <outcome of its last attempt>`, and then the same final `end <clock>` line.
38: 
39: A declared job nothing submits never runs and appears nowhere.
40: 
41: ## Failures
42: 
43: Every refusal writes one line to standard error and exits 2, having written nothing to standard output; the first failure stops the run. A grammar failure names its 1-based log line: `error: line 2: unknown directive cancel`. The messages are `expected limit <starts> <window>`, `expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...`, `expected submit <at> <id>`, `invalid job id <id>`, `invalid outcome <word>`, `<field> must be a non-negative integer` and `<field> must be a positive integer` naming `at`, `duration`, `starts` or `window`, `job <id> is declared twice`, `job <id> is submitted twice`, `limit is declared twice`, and `unknown directive <word>`. A `submit` line naming a job no `job` line declares is refused without a line number, as `error: unknown job <id>`. A malformed argument list is refused with the usage line.
44: 
45: ## Known gaps
46: 
47: A failure is the end of a job: there is no retry, no backoff, and nowhere for a job that never succeeds to go. The rate limit and nothing else can be configured, it can only come from the log itself, and there is no way to run the same log under a different policy.

1: /** The log grammar: the directives, and the failures each one words. */
2: 
3: const ID = /^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]+$/
4: const DIGITS = /^[0-9]+$/
5: 
6: /** One refusal of an input line, carrying the 1-based line, or 0 when the failure names none. */
7: export class LogError extends Error {
8:   /**
9:    * @param {number} line - the 1-based input line, or 0 when the failure names no line.
10:    * @param {string} message - the message the specification words, without the position.
11:    */
12:   constructor(line, message) {
13:     super(message)
14:     this.name = 'LogError'
15:     this.line = line
16:   }
17: }
18: 
19: /**
20:  * Every input line, with the empty tail a trailing newline leaves dropped.
21:  * @param {string} text - the whole input.
22:  * @returns {string[]} the lines.
23:  */
24: export function splitLines(text) {
25:   const split = text.split('\n')
26:   if (split.length > 0 && split[split.length - 1] === '') split.pop()
27:   return split
28: }
29: 
30: /** One field read as a non-negative integer, or the failure that names it. */
31: function count(line, field, word) {
32:   if (!DIGITS.test(word)) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a non-negative integer`)
33:   return Number(word)
34: }
35: 
36: /** One field read as a positive integer, or the failure that names it. */
37: function positive(line, field, word) {
38:   const value = count(line, field, word)
39:   if (value < 1) throw new LogError(line, `${field} must be a positive integer`)
40:   return value
41: }
42: 
43: /**
44:  * Parse the job log.
45:  * @param {string[]} lines - the input lines.
46:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the policy the log sets, edited in place.
47:  * @returns {{jobs: Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>, submissions: {id: string, at: number}[]}} the declared jobs and the submissions in input order.
48:  * @throws {LogError} on the first line the grammar refuses.
49:  */
50: export function parse(lines, policy) {
51:   const jobs = new Map()
52:   const submissions = []
53:   const submitted = new Map()
54:   for (const [index, raw] of lines.entries()) {
55:     const line = index + 1
56:     const text = raw.trim()
57:     if (text === '' || text.startsWith('#')) continue
58:     const words = text.split(/\s+/u)
59:     if (words[0] === 'limit') {
60:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected limit <starts> <window>')
61:       if (policy.limit !== undefined) throw new LogError(line, 'limit is declared twice')
62:       policy.limit = { starts: positive(line, 'starts', words[1]), window: positive(line, 'window', words[2]) }
63:     } else if (words[0] === 'job') {
64:       if (words.length < 4) throw new LogError(line, 'expected job <id> <duration> <outcome>...')
65:       const id = words[1]
66:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
67:       if (jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is declared twice`)
68:       const duration = count(line, 'duration', words[2])
69:       for (const outcome of words.slice(3)) {
70:         if (outcome !== 'ok' && outcome !== 'fail') throw new LogError(line, `invalid outcome ${outcome}`)
71:       }
72:       jobs.set(id, { id, duration, outcomes: words.slice(3) })
73:     } else if (words[0] === 'submit') {
74:       if (words.length !== 3) throw new LogError(line, 'expected submit <at> <id>')
75:       const at = count(line, 'at', words[1])
76:       const id = words[2]
77:       if (!ID.test(id)) throw new LogError(line, `invalid job id ${id}`)
78:       if (submitted.has(id)) throw new LogError(line, `job ${id} is submitted twice`)
79:       submitted.set(id, line)
80:       submissions.push({ id, at })
81:     } else {
82:       throw new LogError(line, `unknown directive ${words[0]}`)
83:     }
84:   }
85:   for (const { id } of submissions) {
86:     if (!jobs.has(id)) throw new LogError(0, `unknown job ${id}`)
87:   }
88:   return { jobs, submissions }
89: }

1: /** The simulation: one worker and a rate limit on starts. */
2: 
3: import { createClock } from './clock.js'
4: 
5: /**
6:  * Run every submission to a verdict.
7:  * @param {Map<string, {id: string, duration: number, outcomes: string[]}>} jobs - the declared jobs.
8:  * @param {{id: string, at: number}[]} submissions - the submissions, in input order.
9:  * @param {{limit?: {starts: number, window: number}}} policy - the rate limit in force.
10:  * @returns {{attempts: {start: number, id: string, attempt: number, outcome: string, finish: number}[], end: number}} the attempts in the order they started and the clock at the end.
11:  */
12: export function run(jobs, submissions, policy) {
13:   const clock = createClock()
14:   const queued = submissions.map((submission, order) => ({ ...submission, order, readyAt: submission.at, attempt: 0 }))
15:   const attempts = []
16:   const starts = []
17:   while (queued.length > 0) {
18:     let pick = 0
19:     for (const [index, entry] of queued.entries()) {
20:       const best = queued[pick]
21:       if (entry.readyAt < best.readyAt || (entry.readyAt === best.readyAt && entry.order < best.order)) pick = index
22:     }
23:     const entry = queued.splice(pick, 1)[0]
24:     clock.advanceTo(entry.readyAt)
25:     if (policy.limit !== undefined && starts.length >= policy.limit.starts) {
26:       const oldest = starts[starts.length - policy.limit.starts]
27:       if (clock.now() - oldest < policy.limit.window) clock.advanceTo(oldest + policy.limit.window)
28:     }
29:     const job = jobs.get(entry.id)
30:     const start = clock.now()
31:     starts.push(start)
32:     const attempt = entry.attempt + 1
33:     const outcome = job.outcomes[Math.min(attempt, job.outcomes.length) - 1]
34:     const finish = start + job.duration
35:     clock.advanceTo(finish)
36:     attempts.push({ start, id: entry.id, attempt, outcome, finish })
37:   }
38:   return { attempts, end: clock.now() }
39: }

11: function fail(message) {
12:   process.stderr.write(`error: ${message}\n`)
13:   process.exit(2)
14: }

16: const argv = process.argv.slice(2)
17: const mode = argv[0]
18: if (!['trace', 'summary'].includes(mode) || argv.length !== 1) fail(USAGE)
19: 
20: const policy = {}
21: let parsed
22: try {
23:   parsed = parse(splitLines(readFileSync(0, 'utf8')), policy)
24: } catch (error) {
25:   if (!(error instanceof LogError)) throw error
26:   fail(error.line === 0 ? error.message : `line ${error.line}: ${error.message}`)
27: }
28: 
29: const { attempts, end } = run(parsed.jobs, parsed.submissions, policy)
30: const out = []
31: if (mode === 'trace') {
32:   for (const one of attempts) out.push(`${one.start} ${one.id} attempt=${one.attempt} ${one.outcome} finish=${one.finish}`)
33: } else {
34:   for (const { id } of [...parsed.submissions].sort((left, right) => (left.id < right.id ? -1 : 1))) {

**`src/parse.js`** — factored the directive bodies into `limitDirective`/`retryDirective` and a `splitWords` helper (trim, skip empty/`#`), so the log and a policy file read the same grammar:

Because it edits the same `policy` object, a log that repeats a directive the policy set fails at the *log's* line with `... is declared twice`.

`jobq` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/jobq.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the retry policy the simulator was built around, somewhere for a job that never succeeds to go, and a way to run one log under a policy that does not live in it. Everything `README.md` documents stays exactly as it is — the log grammar, the simulation, the `trace` and `summary` output, and every failure message and exit code — and the work spans the parser, the simulation, and the command.

`retry <max> <base>` joins the log's directives, parsed like `limit`: exactly two words after it, `<max>` a positive integer and `<base>` a non-negative one, at most one such line, and the same failures as the others, worded `expected retry <max> <base>`, `max must be a positive integer`, `base must be a non-negative integer` and `retry is declared twice`. The directive turns the policy on. With no `retry` line anywhere a job still gets one attempt and a failure is simply final, exactly as today.

Under a retry policy, an attempt that finishes `fail` goes back in the queue when its attempt number is below `<max>`, ready at the instant it failed plus `<base>` multiplied by two raised to the power of one less than that attempt number, so the first backoff is `<base>`, the second twice that, the third four times. A re-queued attempt competes for the worker like any other: it is taken when its ready time is the smallest, ties still break by submission order, and its start still waits out the rate limit. An attempt that finishes `fail` at attempt `<max>` is dead-lettered instead, at the instant it failed.

`dead` is a new mode. It prints one line per dead-lettered job in the order the jobs were written off, `<id> attempts=<n> at=<instant>`, and then a final line `total <k>` counting them. `conflayers` is the repository in this workspace: `README.md` describes what it already does, `src/` holds it, and `test/conflayers.test.js` is its own suite, which passes. Add the two layered modes its `merge` primitive was built for, make the declared types real, and report a bad value where it was written. Everything `README.md` documents about `dump`, `get`, the INI grammar and the existing failures stays exactly as it is, including every message and every column; the work spans the parser, the schema, the layer stack, and the command.

`load <base> <site>` and `origin <base> <site>` each stack three layers, weakest first: the INI file named by the first argument, the INI file named by the second, and an environment layer read from standard input. A later layer overrides a key an earlier one set, one key at a time, so a file that sets only `server.port` leaves every other key to the layer below it. The layers are read in that order, and a layer's failures are all reported before the next layer is read.

The environment layer is a line per variable. A line is trimmed first; an empty one, and one beginning with `#`, is ignored. The rest is `NAME=VALUE`: the text before the first `=` is the name, trimmed, and everything after it is the value, trimmed. A setting travels under `CONF_` followed by its key uppercased with every `.` replaced by `_`, so `server.port` arrives as `CONF_SERVER_PORT`. Its failures carry a position too, worded `error: <stdin>:<line>:<column>: ` followed by `expected NAME=VALUE` or `expected a variable name` or `unknown environment variable <NAME>` or `<NAME> is set twice`, each reported at the line's first non-space character and each counting columns the way the INI parser does.

Both modes are strict about keys where `dump` is lenient: a key an INI layer sets and the schema does not know fails with `error: <file>:<line>:<column>: unknown setting <key>` at the value's position, and a layer's keys are checked in the order the file writes them, after that file parses. The value's position is the column of its first character, or, when the value is empty, one past the line's last non-space character.

`origin <base> <site>` prints `<key> <layer>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the layer is `base`, `site`, `env`, or `default` when no layer set the key.

`load <base> <site>` prints `<key>=<value>` for every schema key in ascending order, where the value is the winning layer's text coerced by the key's declared type, or the schema default coerced the same way. A `string` is its text. An `integer` is an optional `-` and then digits without a leading zero, unless the number is exactly `0`, and renders as written. A `boolean` is `true` or `false`, lowercase, and renders as written. An `enum` is one of its declared members and renders as written. A `duration` is digits followed by `ms`, `s`, `m` or `h`, and renders as its whole number of milliseconds. A `list` is items separated by commas, each trimmed, with a repeat dropped and the order kept, rendered joined by single commas; empty text is the empty list and renders empty, but an empty item between two commas is a failure. A value that does not fit its type fails with `error: <where>: <message>`, where `<where>` is the file and position it was written at, or `<stdin>` and its position when the environment layer set it, and the message is `<key> is not an integer: <text>`, `<key> is not a boolean: <text>`, `<key> is not one of <members joined by |>: <text>`, `<key> is not a duration: <text>` or `<key> has an empty item: <text>`. The keys are coerced in ascending order, so the first failing key in that order decides.

The usage line every malformed argument list reports becomes `error: usage: cli.js dump <file>|get <file> <key>|load <base> <site>|origin <base> <site>`; `dump` takes one path, `get` a path and a key, and `load` and `origin` exactly two paths.
